h: פָּרָשַׁת הַחֹדֶשׁ, מַאֲמָר ד׳ Parshas HaChodesh — Maamar Daled

p: 'The Holy One, blessed be He, told me:
Say to them, I have surely remembered you,'
it is not yet the time of remembrance;
what is my strength, that I should hope?
Is my strength the strength of stones?' etc.
they said, 'This is a good sign' —
'and a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.'"
We need to understand what this expression means,
הוּא מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסִיקְתָּא [שָׁם סִימָן ז]
is what they said in the Pesikta (ibid. siman 7)
and in the Midrash (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:21):
when the land of Mitzrayim is full
of the filth of our idolatry?' etc.
'He does not look at your deeds;
מְדַלֵּג עַל הֶהָרִים [שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ב, ח]
וְאֵין הָרִים אֶלָּא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כּוּלֵּי
and "mountains" means nothing but idolatry' etc.
when we have no deeds in our hands?' etc.
'He does not look at your evil deeds.'
such as Amram and his beis din'" etc.;
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר תּוֹחֶלֶת מְמוּשָּׁכָה כּוּלֵּי
And about this he said, "Hope deferred" etc.,
"What is my strength, that I should hope?" —
since we have no good deeds,
and on the contrary, we have the opposite,
"what is my strength, that I should hope"
And even if they improve their deeds,
there is no guarantee for tzaddikim in this world;
and we saw that there entered Mitzrayim
Yaakov and his offspring, the tribes of Kah,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם זַרְעָם נִתְקַלְקְלוּ כָּל כָּךְ
and nonetheless their descendants became so corrupted
and sank into the kelipah of Mitzrayim.
And who is greater for us than Yaakov Avinu,
peace be upon him, who was promised,
וּשְׁמַרְתִּיךָ בְּכָל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלֵךְ [בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, טו]
"And I will guard you wherever you go" (Bereishis 28:15),
and they said "will cause," in the future tense —
for he did not trust himself.
וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר
And likewise David HaMelech, peace be upon him, said:
אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ אִם יֵשׁ לִי חֵלֶק בֵּינֵיהֶם
"I do not know whether I have a share among them
which applies even when they were promised,
And even a span of fifteen days
כְּתִיב [שְׁמוֹת י, כג] וּלְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
it is written (Shemos 10:23), "And for all the Children of Yisrael
And we have said that the plagues went
and it was in the secret of
(עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב לו, א)
(along the lines of what they said, Zohar II 36a);
and with each plague Yisrael came out
which is the utterance "Let there be light,"
"and for all the Children of Yisrael there was light"
(and it was explained in Parshas Bo, maamar 2).
And in the utterance "Let there be light"
corresponding to the five Chumashim of the Torah
where the words of Torah already begin,
"The Torah should not have needed to begin
except from 'This month shall be for you,'"
they said, "This is a good sign,"
and did not say "a good promise,"
for there is no guarantee in this world,
as mentioned above, "perhaps sin will cause it";
"and a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" —
"tree of life" means nothing but Torah
the shining forth of words of Torah:
the moon that receives from the sun,
and they sensed the light from the sun as well,
"For a sun and a shield is Hashem" etc.;
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק א רב, א)
and they said, "This is a good sign"
And then they merited the attribute of Knesses Yisrael,
that is, "I am Hashem who dwells
in the midst of the Children of Yisrael,"
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
for the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Yisrael,
and my portion is God forever"
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב)
and it is a good sign
that they will be able to remove and empty out the evil
from "the heart of the fool, at his left,"
and that holiness and words of Torah will enter
"the heart of the wise, at his right,"
And this is the point of Parshas HaChodesh:
that they should sense this holiness.
And we read it on Shabbos,
for it is stated (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 48):
who makes for them on Shabbos
a dwelling in the two chambers of the heart" etc.;
and they can merit the light
of the coming Rosh Chodesh and Yom Tov;
and it is a good sign
that in Nissan they are redeemed.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 15 — “‘Hope prolonged makes the heart sick’ refers to Israel before they were redeemed. When Moshe came to Israel and said, ‘The Holy One, blessed be He, told me: Go, tell Israel, I have surely remembered you,’ they said: ‘Moshe Rabbeinu, is it not yet the time of remembrance? What is my strength, that I should hope? Is my strength the strength of stones? Is our flesh made of bronze?’ Once he told them, ‘In this month you are redeemed,’ they said: ‘This is a good sign; a tree of life is desire fulfilled.’” The passage expressly calls the announcement a good sign. Rav Tzadok asks why it describes a sign rather than merely a favorable promise. The verses woven into the Midrash are Mishlei 13:12, Shemos 3:16, and Iyov 6:11–12.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah, on 2:8 — “When Moshe told Israel, ‘In this month you are redeemed,’ they said: ‘Moshe Rabbeinu, how can we be redeemed when we have no good deeds?’ He replied: ‘Since He desires your redemption, He does not look at your evil deeds. At whom does He look? At the righteous among you and their deeds, such as Amram and his court.’ ... The Sages say: They said, ‘How can we be redeemed when all Egypt is defiled with our idolatry?’ He replied: ‘Since He desires your redemption, He does not look at your idolatry, but leaps over the mountains; mountains here mean idolatry.’” These are two distinct explanations in the Midrash: one invokes the righteous among Israel, and another God’s desire to redeem despite their idolatry. Together they frame the anxiety about Israel’s lack of merit.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rashi on Bereishis 32:11 — “My merits have been lessened by the kindness You did me; so I fear that since You promised me I have become soiled with sin, and it may cause me to be handed to Esav.” Rashi shows that Yaakov did not doubt the promise. He feared for himself. That is exactly why a promise in this world is no guarantee.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 4a — “David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: ‘Master of the world, I am confident that You will pay a good reward to the righteous in the future, but I do not know whether I have a share among them or not’—lest sin cause it. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raised a contradiction: It is written, ‘I am with you and will guard you wherever you go,’ but it is also written, ‘Yaakov was very afraid.’ He said: ‘Lest sin cause it.’” The Gemara applies this concern both to David and to Yaakov. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the future tense: fear of a possible lapse can remain even after an assurance.

paragraphs.text: Exodus 10:23 — “They did not see one another, and no one rose from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.” The verse contrasts the Egyptians’ darkness with Israel’s light. Rav Tzadok develops the latter as an inward illumination accompanying the plague.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Va'eira 5 — “The plagues of Egypt were ten, and everywhere ten points to the ten sefiros; with each plague Yisrael left one of the ten kelipos that stand opposite, and entered one attribute in holiness.” Rav Tzadok there cites Zohar II 29a, “HaKadosh Baruch Hu began from below.” This is the source for the order from below to above. That order is why the ninth plague, against Chochmah, brought light.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 32b — “What is the remedy? Let him engage in Torah, as it is said: ‘A tree of life is desire fulfilled’; and a tree of life means only Torah, as it is said: ‘It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it.’” The discussion concerns the heartache of disappointed expectation in prayer. Its remedy through Torah is particularly apt to Rav Tzadok’s reading of prolonged hope and the good sign of redemption.

paragraphs.text: Psalms 84:12 — “For Hashem God is a sun and a shield; Hashem grants favor and honor. He withholds no good from those who walk wholeheartedly.” Rav Tzadok draws on the image of the sun in explaining an illumination that reaches the moon, his image here for the Oral Torah.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5 — “‘Fortunate is one who makes them a dwelling in the two chambers of the heart, and the yetzer hara is cleared from there’: the yetzer hara sits between the two openings of the heart.” The Gemara cited there is Berachos 61a. Holiness dwelling in both chambers leaves the yetzer no place, and this is what Rav Tzadok says of the heart’s left side.
